classification.difficultyReason: Part f requires selecting the reflex central angle corresponding to the given circumference angle, converting it to the minor angle, and combining tangent-radius perpendicularity with the quadrilateral angle sum.

spec.description: Inscribed isosceles triangle with matching double chord ticks and a tangent at the lower-right vertex.
spec.mathematics: The upper-right interior angle is 55 degrees; a is the angle between the tangent's rightward ray and the vertical chord.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the supplied 55-degree angle and unknown a are visible.

answer.worked:
The base angles of the isosceles triangle are both $55^\circ$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Remaining angle}&=180^\circ-55^\circ-55^\circ\\&=70^\circ\\a&=70^\circ\end{aligned}$$
The angle between the tangent and chord equals the angle in the alternate segment.

spec.description: Inscribed triangle with matching double ticks on its left and bottom chords; tangent at its upper-left vertex.
spec.mathematics: The angle between equal chords is 80 degrees. The unknown lies between the tangent's lower-left ray and the left chord.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the supplied 80-degree angle and unknown a are visible.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Each base angle}&=\frac{180^\circ-80^\circ}{2}\\&=50^\circ\\a&=50^\circ\end{aligned}$$
The base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal. The alternate segment theorem gives $a=50^\circ$.

spec.description: Tangent at the top of a circle, a diameter through a marked centre and an inscribed triangle. A pointer identifies the given angle at the lower-right vertex.
spec.mathematics: The lower-right angle is 73 degrees; a is the tangent–chord angle at the top contact point.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the supplied 73-degree angle and unknown a are visible.

answer.worked: $a=73^\circ$ by the alternate segment theorem: the angle between the tangent and chord equals the angle in the alternate segment.

spec.description: Two tangents meet below the circle. A diameter joins the left contact point to an upper-right vertex; a chord and radius join the right contact point.
spec.mathematics: The upper-right inscribed angle is 70 degrees. The external angle between tangents is a.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the supplied 70-degree angle and unknown a are visible.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Angle at the centre}&=2\times70^\circ\\&=140^\circ\\a&=360^\circ-90^\circ-90^\circ-140^\circ\\&=40^\circ\end{aligned}$$
The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference on the same arc. Each tangent is perpendicular to its radius, and the angles of a quadrilateral sum to $360^\circ$.

spec.description: Two tangents meet above a circle. Their contact points are joined by a chord and by radii to O. A curved pointer identifies the unknown at the left contact point.
spec.mathematics: The tangent angle is 38 degrees. The unknown a is between the chord and left radius, not at the centre.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the supplied 38-degree angle and unknown a are visible.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Angle at the centre}&=360^\circ-90^\circ-90^\circ-38^\circ\\&=142^\circ\\a&=\frac{180^\circ-142^\circ}{2}\\&=19^\circ\end{aligned}$$
Tangents meet radii at $90^\circ$. The two radii form an isosceles triangle, so its base angles are equal.

spec.description: A vertical tangent at the left contact and a second tangent meet below the circle. Radii meet at a marked centre; two chords form an inscribed angle on the lower minor arc.
spec.mathematics: The inscribed angle is 117 degrees and stands on the major arc between the contact points. The external tangent angle is a.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the supplied 117-degree angle and unknown a are visible.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Reflex angle at the centre}&=2\times117^\circ\\&=234^\circ\\\text{Minor angle at the centre}&=360^\circ-234^\circ\\&=126^\circ\\a&=360^\circ-90^\circ-90^\circ-126^\circ\\&=54^\circ\end{aligned}$$
The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference on the same arc. Each tangent meets its radius at $90^\circ$.
